mcqs.question: You're encoding a `city` column with 5,000 unique values for a gradient boosting model. One-hot encoding would add 5,000 columns. What's a better default, and what's its main risk?
options: Target encoding — risk is label leakage if not done with proper cross-validation or smoothing
Ordinal encoding by alphabetical order — this is always safe since it's just integers
One-hot encoding anyway — the only downside is somewhat slower training
Dropping the column entirely — always the safest choice for high-cardinality features
mcqs.explanation: Target encoding stays compact regardless of cardinality but leaks the label into the feature unless computed with held-out folds or smoothing. Alphabetical ordinal encoding invents a false numeric order the model will wrongly treat as meaningful. One-hot at 5,000 categories causes sparsity and overfitting, not just slower training. Dropping the column throws away potentially real signal.

mcqs.question: Which model is least affected by leaving numeric features unscaled?
options: K-nearest neighbors
Logistic regression trained with gradient descent
Random forest
SVM with an RBF kernel
mcqs.explanation: Random forest splits each feature on its own threshold independently of other features' magnitudes, so scaling doesn't change its decisions. KNN and RBF-kernel SVM rely on distance calculations, and gradient descent on logistic regression converges unevenly when feature magnitudes differ wildly — all three are sensitive to scale.

mcqs.question: A loan dataset has a `previous_default` field missing for 15% of applicants, and those missing rows correlate strongly with the loan outcome. What should you probably do?
options: Drop those rows, since more than 10% missing invalidates the feature
Impute with the mode and move on — once it's filled in, missingness no longer matters
Impute the value and also add a `was_missing` binary flag, since the missingness pattern itself looks predictive
Always impute missing numeric-like fields with 0, since 0 is a neutral default
mcqs.explanation: When missingness correlates with the target, the fact that a value is missing is itself a signal worth keeping as a feature, alongside a reasonable imputed value. Dropping 15% of rows that aren't random would bias the dataset. Treating imputation as the end of the story throws away that signal. 0 isn't inherently neutral — it can look like a real, misleading value.

mcqs.question: Which feature selection approach removes features by shrinking their coefficients to exactly zero as part of model training itself?
options: Filter methods using correlation scores
Wrapper methods using recursive feature elimination
Embedded methods using L1 (Lasso) regularization
Embedded methods using L2 (Ridge) regularization
mcqs.explanation: L1/Lasso's penalty pushes unhelpful coefficients to exactly zero as training proceeds, pruning features as a byproduct of fitting. L2/Ridge shrinks coefficients but rarely to exactly zero, so it regularizes without truly selecting. Filter and wrapper methods are separate stages that run before or around training, not embedded in it.

mcqs.question: You fit a StandardScaler on your entire dataset, then split into train/test, then train your model. Test accuracy looks great. What's wrong?
options: Nothing — scalers don't touch the target, so there's no leakage risk
The scaler's mean and std were computed using test-set rows, leaking test-set distribution info into the training features
StandardScaler is incompatible with train/test splitting; only min-max scaling should be used
Nothing — leakage only applies to target encoding, not to scaling
mcqs.explanation: Even though the scaler never sees the label, computing its mean/std over the full dataset means test-set values shaped the transform applied to training data — a real, if subtler, form of leakage that inflates reported metrics. It's not about which scaler you pick; any transform fit before splitting has this problem, including target encoding.
